newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa ready to drop Rwanda arms deal.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa ready to drop Rwanda arms deal.

text.p: South Africa is willing to scrap a controversial deal to sell arms to Rwanda if Central and East African governments ask it to do so, a senior government minister said on Monday.

Kader Asmal, chairman of the National Conventional Arms Control Committee that vets weapons exports, said the government would be guided by leaders of the Great Lakes states. The leaders were due to meet on Tuesday in Nairobi to discuss fighting in eastern Zaire.
"We have to be very calm and correct. We'll wait for the Great Lakes discussion tomorrow. We will follow the advice of the Great Lakes region," Asmal told reporters in Cape Town.

He said his arms control committee would meet on November 14, but added that he and Defence Minister Joe Modise could cancel or suspend the Rwanda contract if this was deemed to be in South Africa's national interest.
South Africa has been widely criticised for agreeing in September to sell vehicles and small arms worth an estimated 86.8 million rand ($18.5 million) to Rwanda's military government.
Rivalry between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis has troubled Rwanda and Burundi for generations, sparking genocidal massacres in 1994.
In the past few weeks in eastern Zaire ethnic Tutsi rebels, with the support of the Rwandan army, have been battling Zairean government troops.
Amnesty International Secretary-General Pierre Sane, on a visit to South Africa, said foreign weapons were being used in abuses carried out by all parties to the fighting.
Weapons and ammunition should be prevented from fuelling an "explosive and catastrophic" situation, he said in a statement.
"It has been widely acknowledged that the area is awash with small arms despite previous commitments by the international community to restrict them," Sane added.
Asmal defended the decision by his committee to approve the South Africa arms sale, but declined to give specific details of the equipment included in the contract.
"It's a very modest figure of exports to Rwanda. The easier decision would have been not to export arms. We decided, on evaluation, that a vacuum is dangerous...that we could supply defensive arms.
"We have only sent armoured personnel carriers so far, and there is no evidence, even circumstantial, that Rwanda has used its arms or military formations in eastern Zaire," he said.

President Nelson Mandela recently rejected a U.S. initiative for a Western-led force of African troops to keep the peace in continental hot-spots. Mandela said such a force should come under United Nations or Organisation of African Unity aegis.
Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils, however, said South Africa would consider speeding up the training of units which might participate in peacekeeping operations in Africa.
"We're really not ready for such a project, but at the same time, how much longer can this country turn a blind eye to the awful carnage, to this explosive situation in Zaire?" he said.
